extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers and authors learning craft, especially those writing adventure stories
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and criteria for conceiving, plotting, and writing adventure stories—what defines the element of adventure, how it differs from related genres, and practical guidance for creating set pieces, protagonists, pacing, and use of environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core definition — thrill of doing
rubrics_metrics.description: The element of adventure evokes “I want to DO that.” It is the thrill of doing something rather than the thrill of seeing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with wonder (thrill of seeing) and idea stories (mental exploration). Adventure's emotional hook is active wish-fulfillment: the reader thinks, “I want to go there and do that!”

rubrics_metrics.name: Source of danger — self-chosen vs external
rubrics_metrics.description: Adventure: the question is “Can I do this?” — trouble you choose, pushing your limits. Thriller: danger is an outside threat coming after you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can have thriller moments inside an adventure, but the genre hinge is where danger arises. Example: Indiana Jones (adventure: he goes for it) vs typical thriller (protagonist being pursued).

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical challenge vs idea-story (mental) challenge
rubrics_metrics.description: Adventure stories are usually built around a physical challenge; idea stories are usually mental challenges or exploration of an idea/place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use physical obstacles, set pieces, stunts and environment-based problems for adventure; reserve idea-driven puzzles and conceptual discovery for idea stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Milieu/setting-driven storytelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Adventure is often based on the milieu — the place or environment supplies opportunities for cool things to do and for set pieces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invent set pieces from the setting (e.g., Antarctica, an asteroid belt, a factory full of flames). Even ordinary settings can work if the set pieces add unique environmental elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist is competent but pushed to the edge
rubrics_metrics.description: Take a competent hero to the edge of their competency so they can almost pull off great things but sometimes fail; show competence first so stakes feel earned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce competence early (Indiana Jones intro example), then create moments where they must improvise or stretch skills; failures or near-fails increase investment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist often an outsider
rubrics_metrics.description: The person having the adventure is frequently an outsider in the setting, which makes familiar places feel exotic and enables discovery and improvisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can set adventure in a familiar place (e.g., Rumble in the Bronx) if the protagonist is not from there; outsider viewpoint allows fresh use of environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set pieces: generate, list, order, and escalate
rubrics_metrics.description: Adventure frequently consists of set piece after set piece — cool action scenes and amazing things to do — which should be identified, ordered, and positioned structurally in the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write a list of set pieces, then order them for pacing and escalation. Use a strong early set piece to promise readers, de-escalate for setup, then build to grander payoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Escalation of stakes and spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the explosions/stunts/stakes bigger (or the solutions cooler) over the course of the story to keep readers pulled from page to page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Escalation can be quantitative (bigger explosions) or qualitative (more personal stakes or cooler problem-solving). Plan payoffs and progressively raise what’s at risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on how the character solves problems — make solutions cool
rubrics_metrics.description: A key part of adventure is not only that bad things happen but how the protagonist deals with them; make the character’s solutions cooler and more inventive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize interesting, character-specific solutions over merely larger dangers. Mary’s note: it’s about making how the character solves it cooler, not just bigger explosions.

rubrics_metrics.name: External conflict is primary (but include internal arc)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflict in an adventure story tends to be external — environment or other people — though characters should still have internal arcs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure external obstacles are compelling and challenging; internal development can run alongside but should not replace the adventure’s external problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvisation and inventive use of environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Adventure demands improvisation: characters should look at a scene and figure out how to use ladders, bottles, walls, vehicles, etc., as tools in set pieces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design fights and action around dynamic, non-level terrain and props so encounters feel cinematic and resourceful (examples: Jackie Chan ladder fight, Princess Bride sword fight).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone shapes genre — lighten or darken to shift audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Changing tone can shift a thriller toward adventure (e.g., lighten tone or ratings changes like PG-13), and vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be conscious which audience you want; a lighter tone emphasizes fun, adventurous wish-fulfillment, while darker tone centers survival and suspense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of setting uniqueness even in ordinary locations
rubrics_metrics.description: Even commonplace settings can become adventure-rich if each set piece adds something unique or extraordinary to the environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alter or emphasize elements (a car launched at a helicopter, a moving platform, a factory of flames and TVs) so ordinary places host extraordinary action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plotting for reader pull — payoffs and pacing
rubrics_metrics.description: When plotting, think of what will pull readers from page to page: early promise, mid-story setup, escalating payoffs, and structural placement of set pieces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan where to place small and large escalations; give readers a good opening hook, then vary tempo to maintain investment and build to major set pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate exposition into action
rubrics_metrics.description: You can and should deliver exposition during exciting events: set an expository scene during something thrilling so the story remains an adventure while informing the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Homework: Take an expository scene (character intro, important info) and set it during something exciting — a room falling apart, an attack, a runaway cart — to keep momentum while conveying necessary information.
